13640: Slaves and powerless members would hear that they had access to the highest presence of all. Gentiles would hear that their story is part of humanity's story from Adam. Jews would hear that the Law's role was real but limited, and that the Messiah has fulfilled Israel's vocation. Everyone would hear 'peace' in contrast with Rome's version.
13641: Romans 5:8 is often quoted rightly as the heart of God's love. The Adam-Christ passage widens the gospel from 'my sins' to 'humanity's story': Jesus starts a new humanity. Different traditions read 5:12 differently: Western churches (following Augustine) see inherited guilt; Eastern Orthodox see inherited mortality and corruption. Both agree Christ's obedience is greater than Adam's fall.
13642: Adam's disobedience brings death into the world, the background to Rom 5:12.
13643: The servant makes 'many' righteous through his obedience; Rom 5:19 echoes 'the many'.
13644: God promises to pour out his Spirit, echoed in love 'poured out' by the Spirit (Rom 5:5).
13645: The messenger who announces peace and says 'your God reigns', the Jewish meaning of peace-as-gospel.
13646: Romans 5:12 proves that each baby is born personally guilty of Adam's sin (a Western doctrine of original guilt).
13647: Paul clearly says sin and death came through Adam and spread to all. How exactly (inherited guilt, inherited corruption, or each person's own sinning, 'because all sinned') is debated between Augustinian, Reformed and Orthodox traditions. Paul's main point is the greater power of Christ's grace.
13648: Changing Masters: Dead to Sin, Alive to God
13649: Should we keep sinning so grace can increase? By no means. Believers were baptised into Christ's death so that they might walk in newness of life, sharing his resurrection. Sin is no longer to reign in their mortal bodies. Using the picture of slavery, Paul says they have changed masters: once slaves of sin, now slaves of righteousness and of God. The wages of sin is death, but the free gift of God is eternal life in Christ Jesus our Lord.
13650: Paul's critics accused his grace-gospel of encouraging moral laxity (3:8). He answers by grounding ethics in union with Christ. Baptism was the moment of transfer into the Messiah's people, probably by immersion, a visible picture of burial and rising.
13651: Slavery was everywhere in Rome; perhaps a third of the city's population were slaves or former slaves. Slaves could be bought, sold, or transferred to new owners; a freed slave owed continuing duties to his patron. Paul says, 'I am speaking in human terms because of your weakness' (6:19): he uses slavery as an analogy his hearers knew in their bodies. 'Wages' (opsōnia) were a soldier's ration-pay; 'gift' (charisma) was a free grant. Paul contrasts what sin pays out with what God gives.
13652: Rom 6 retells the Exodus. Israel passed through the sea (which Paul elsewhere calls a 'baptism', 1 Cor 10:2), leaving slavery in Egypt to serve God. Believers pass through baptism, leaving slavery to sin to serve God. 'Present yourselves to God' (6:13) uses the language of offering. 'Newness of life' fits the prophetic hope of new creation. The goal is holiness (6:19, 6:22), what Torah always aimed at: 'you shall be holy, for I am holy'.
13653: Slaves and freedpeople would feel this chapter keenly: they knew what it meant to change owners, and what it cost. Gentile converts from pagan cults, which also had initiation rites, would hear that baptism means death to the old life, not just a ritual. Jewish believers concerned that Paul's gospel was lawless would hear Paul insisting on holiness.
13654: Romans 6:23 is usually preached to unbelievers. In context it is said to believers: you have a new master; do not go back to the old one. Grace is not a loophole but a new allegiance. The chapter also invites careful thought about how slavery imagery lands for descendants of enslaved peoples: Paul uses it to speak of liberation, not to endorse the institution.
13655: Israel passes through the sea from slavery to freedom; Paul links this to baptism (1 Cor 10:1-2).
13656: Redeemed Israel becomes God's treasured possession and holy nation: freed to serve God.
13657: 'You shall be holy': the goal of 'slavery to righteousness leading to holiness' (Rom 6:19).
13658: God opens Israel's graves and gives life by his Spirit, background to 'newness of life'.
13659: Romans 6:23 is an evangelistic verse explaining that unbelievers deserve death but can receive eternal life.
13660: That truth is in Romans, but 6:23 concludes an argument to baptised believers: you have changed masters, so live under the new one. It is about the shape of a believer's life, as much as about entry into salvation.
13661: The Law Is Holy, but Sin Hijacked It
13662: Using marriage as an illustration, Paul says believers have died to the Law through the body of Christ, so they now belong to the risen one and serve in the new way of the Spirit. Is the Law sin, then? No: the Law is holy, and the commandment holy, just and good. But sin seized the commandment and used it to bring death. An anguished 'I' wants to do the good the Law commands but cannot, and cries out: 'Who will rescue me from this body of death?' Thanks be to God through Jesus Christ.
13663: Paul writes to 'those who know the law' (7:1), probably both Jewish believers and Gentiles who had learned Torah in synagogues. Having said that believers are 'not under law but under grace' (6:14), Paul must explain why he is not attacking God's Law. Debate over the identity of the 'I' in 7:7-25 goes back to the early church: many early Greek writers took it as a person without Christ; Augustine changed his mind and read it as a Christian; Luther and Calvin followed him.
13664: Ancient writers used 'speech-in-character' (prosopopoeia): an author speaks in the voice of someone else to dramatise a situation. Greco-Roman moralists also wrote about the divided self, knowing the good but not doing it (Medea's lament in Euripides and Ovid was famous). Paul's audience would recognise this kind of speech. Roman marriage law, in which a wife was bound to her husband until his death, provides the opening illustration.
13665: The 'I' echoes Adam in Eden: one commandment, sin like a serpent seizing the opportunity, deception, and death (compare 7:11 with Gen 3:13). It also echoes Israel at Sinai: receiving the holy Law and almost at once breaking it with the golden calf. Paul insists the Law is God's good gift (7:12, 7:14); the problem lies in 'sin dwelling in me' and the weakness of the flesh. This is not a Jewish complaint against Torah, which Jews celebrated as delight (Ps 19; Ps 119), but a diagnosis of what the Law alone cannot do without the promised Spirit.
13666: Jewish believers would hear Paul defend the Law's holiness, which they needed to hear. They might recognise Israel's own story of failure. Gentile believers attracted to adopting the Law would hear that taking it on would not solve the problem of sin. Both are being set up for chapter 8's answer.
13667: Many Christians find Rom 7 deeply true to their experience of struggle, and every reading agrees struggle with sin is real. The question is whether this passage describes the normal, defeated condition of a believer, or life under the Law without the Spirit, answered in chapter 8. Reading 7 and 8 together keeps both honesty and hope.
13668: 'The serpent deceived me': sin 'deceived me' through the commandment (Rom 7:11).
13669: 'You shall not covet': the commandment Paul cites in Rom 7:7.
13670: Israel turns to the golden calf right after receiving the Law, a pattern behind 'when the commandment came, sin revived'.
13671: The Law of the Lord is perfect: the Jewish delight in Torah Paul affirms in Rom 7:12 and 7:22.
13672: Romans 7:14-25 describes the mature Christian's normal life: always wanting to do good and always failing.
13673: This is a long-running scholarly debate, not simply a popular error. Many scholars (Kümmel, Moo, Wright, Stowers) think the 'I' is someone under the Law without the Spirit, such as Adam or Israel, voiced dramatically. Others (Augustine, Luther, Calvin, Packer, Dunn in part) see the believer's ongoing struggle. All agree chapter 8 is Paul's answer and that Rom 7 is no excuse for giving up.
13674: Life in the Spirit and the Renewal of Creation
13675: There is now no condemnation for those in Christ Jesus. God has done what the Law, weakened by the flesh, could not do: by sending his Son as a sin offering, he condemned sin in the flesh, so that the Law's just requirement is fulfilled in those who walk by the Spirit. The Spirit makes believers God's children and heirs, crying 'Abba, Father'. All creation groans, waiting for the revealing of God's children. God works all things together for good for those who love him, and nothing in all creation can separate us from God's love in Christ.
13676: Chapter 8 is the climax of Rom 5-8. Suffering is assumed throughout: believers 'suffer with him' (8:17) and face 'tribulation, distress, persecution, famine, nakedness, danger, sword' (8:35). About seven years later, in AD 64, Nero would blame Rome's Christians for the great fire and execute many of them, as Tacitus reports. Paul's words would be read by people who soon needed them.
13677: Adoption (huiothesia) in Roman law was a legal act, often of an adult, transferring someone into a new family with full rights of inheritance; old debts were cancelled. Roman emperors were often adopted heirs (Augustus by Julius Caesar, Nero by Claudius). For slaves in the church, being made 'heirs of God and co-heirs with Christ' was astonishing. 'Abba' is Aramaic for 'father', the intimate word Jesus used (Mark 14:36), kept in a Greek letter to Rome.
13678: Rom 8 is a new Exodus and a return from exile. Israel was God's 'firstborn son' (Exod 4:22), led by God's presence through the wilderness to an inheritance. Now the Spirit leads God's children (8:14) towards an inheritance that is the whole renewed creation. The prophets promised that God would put his Spirit within his people so they would walk in his ways (Ezek 36:26-27) and that the creation itself would be renewed (Isa 65:17). 'Who will bring a charge against God's elect? It is God who justifies' (8:33) echoes Isa 50:8. 'For your sake we are killed all day long' (8:36) is from Ps 44, Israel's lament of faithful suffering.
13679: Slaves and the poor would hear that they were heirs of the world. Gentile believers would hear Israel's titles (sons, firstborn, elect, called, glorified) applied to them, which raises the urgent question of chapter 9: what about Israel itself? Jewish believers would hear their ancestral hope of the Spirit and new creation being fulfilled.
13680: Rom 8:28 is beloved but often misused as a promise that everything will turn out pleasant. In context, the 'good' is being shaped into the image of God's Son (8:29), and the setting is suffering, groaning and persecution. Romans 8 also gives Christians a strong reason to care for creation: God plans to liberate it, not discard it.
13681: God promises a new heart and his Spirit within, so his people walk in his statutes: fulfilled in Rom 8:4.
13682: Israel is God's firstborn son, the background to adoption and 'firstborn among many brothers'.
13683: Abraham did not withhold his son; 'he who did not spare his own Son' (Rom 8:32) echoes the binding of Isaac.
13684: 'He who vindicates me is near; who will contend with me?' echoed in Rom 8:33-34.
13685: A lament of faithful Israel suffering 'for your sake', quoted in Rom 8:36.
13686: Romans 8:28 means God will make everything in my life turn out well, in the way I hope.
13687: The 'good' is defined in 8:29: being conformed to the image of God's Son. The promise holds in the middle of real suffering (8:18, 8:35-36), not in avoiding it. It is a promise of God's faithful purpose for his people, not of comfort on demand.
13688: Has God's Word Failed? Israel, Promise and Mercy
13689: Paul expresses deep anguish for his fellow Jews, to whom belong the adoption, the glory, the covenants, the Law, the worship, the promises, the patriarchs and the Messiah himself. Has God's word failed? No: not all descended from Israel are Israel, and God's promise has always worked by calling, not by human descent or effort, as in the choice of Isaac and Jacob. Using Exodus and the potter image, Paul defends God's freedom to show mercy. Now God has called a people from Jews and Gentiles, while Israel stumbled over the stone, seeking righteousness as if by works.
13690: Romans 9-11 is not a detour. After the soaring promises of chapter 8, the obvious question in Rome was: if God's promises are so sure, why have most of Paul's fellow Jews not accepted Jesus as Messiah? Gentile believers in Rome may have begun to conclude that God had moved on from Israel. Paul's argument here is the background to many later Christian attitudes to Jews, both good and terrible.
13691: Paul speaks as a member of a people under accusation. His willingness to be 'cursed and cut off' for his kin (9:3) echoes the loyalty expected within a kinship group. The potter image (9:20-23) was common in the ancient world for a creator's authority. Honour and shame appear again: 'whoever believes in him will not be put to shame' (9:33).
13692: Paul retells Israel's story in order: Abraham and Isaac (Gen 21:12), Jacob and Esau (Gen 25:23; Mal 1:2-3), Moses and Pharaoh (Exod 33:19; 9:16), Hosea's promise that 'not my people' will be called 'my people' (Hos 2:23), and Isaiah's remnant (Isa 10:22; 1:9). Moses' own prayer to be blotted out for Israel (Exod 32:32) lies behind 9:3. This is an intra-Jewish argument about God's faithfulness, of the kind the prophets made. 'Jacob I loved, Esau I hated' in Malachi refers to the peoples Israel and Edom; 'hated' in Hebrew idiom can mean 'chose not' rather than emotional hatred.
13693: Jewish believers would feel Paul's grief as their own, and also the honour of the list of Israel's privileges (9:4-5). Gentile believers would hear that their inclusion is pure mercy, foretold in Hosea, giving no ground for pride. Everyone would wrestle with the hard questions about God's justice that Paul himself raises (9:14, 9:19).
13694: Rom 9 has been at the centre of debates about predestination since Augustine. It should also be read as a chapter about God's faithfulness to Israel and as an example of grief for others. Christians who read it should share Paul's love for the Jewish people, not use it to justify contempt.
13695: Moses asks to be blotted out of God's book for Israel's sake, like Paul's wish in Rom 9:3.
13696: 'Jacob I loved, Esau I hated': about the nations Israel and Edom, quoted in Rom 9:13.
13697: 'I will have mercy on whom I have mercy', God's self-description after the golden calf, quoted in Rom 9:15.
13698: 'Not my people' become 'my people': a promise to restore Israel that Paul sees widening to Gentiles.
13699: A stone laid in Zion: whoever trusts will not be put to shame (Rom 9:33).
13700: Romans 9 is mainly a proof text about God choosing which individuals will be eternally saved or lost.
13701: Scholars disagree here (see the misreadings list). Some, like Piper and Schreiner, see individual election to salvation; others, like Wright and Dunn, see God's calling of peoples to roles in his purpose. Either way, the chapter's question is God's faithfulness to Israel, and its story ends in mercy for all (11:32). Reading it apart from chapters 10-11 distorts it.
13702: The Word Is Near You: Jesus Is Lord
13703: Paul prays for Israel's salvation. They have zeal for God, but not according to knowledge, seeking to establish their own righteousness rather than submitting to God's. The Messiah is the 'end' (telos: goal or end) of the Law for righteousness for everyone who believes. Reading Deuteronomy 30, Paul says the 'word of faith' is near: if you confess with your mouth that Jesus is Lord and believe in your heart that God raised him from the dead, you will be saved. There is no distinction between Jew and Greek; everyone who calls on the Lord's name will be saved. So messengers must be sent.
13704: Paul's own past as a 'zealous' persecutor of the church (Gal 1:13-14; Phil 3:6) lies behind 10:2. Zeal had a heroic tradition in Judaism (Phinehas, Elijah, the Maccabees). Paul knows it from inside. This chapter also prepares for his request: he wants Rome's help to send him to Spain (15:24), the 'ends of the world' to which the gospel must go.
13705: Confessing 'Jesus is Lord' (Kyrios Iēsous) in Rome was a public loyalty statement. Emperors were increasingly called kyrios; later, Christians were executed for refusing to say 'Caesar is Lord'. 'Beautiful feet' of messengers (10:15) recalls runners who brought news of a victory or a new king. Calling on a name meant appealing to a patron or god for help.
13706: Deut 30:11-14 says God's commandment is not too far away, 'not in heaven, not beyond the sea; the word is very near you, in your mouth and in your heart'. Moses said this in the context of a promised return after exile (Deut 30:1-6). Paul reads it as fulfilled in the Messiah: the word now near is the message of faith. 'Everyone who calls on the name of the LORD will be saved' (Joel 2:32) originally means YHWH; Paul applies it to Jesus, placing him within Israel's worship of the one God. Isaiah's messenger of good news (Isa 52:7) announces Zion's return and God's reign. Deut 32 and Isa 65 explain Israel's surprising unbelief and Gentile inclusion.
13707: Jewish believers heard their own Torah (Deuteronomy) and prophets (Isaiah, Joel) read as pointing to Jesus. Gentile believers heard that they had equal access: 'there is no distinction'. Both were drawn into Paul's mission: if all who call will be saved, someone must be sent, and Rome could help send Paul.
13708: Romans 10:9-10 is central to evangelism, and rightly so. In context it is also a public allegiance to Jesus as Lord, which in Rome had political edge, and a fulfilment of Israel's story. 'Christ is the end of the law' (10:4) is best understood as the Law's goal and climax, not its abolition in contempt.
13709: 'The word is very near you': Moses' promise of return, read by Paul as the message of faith in the Messiah.
13710: 'Whoever calls on the name of the LORD will be saved', applied by Paul to Jesus as Lord.
13711: How beautiful are the feet of the messenger who announces peace and says 'Your God reigns'.
13712: 'Lord, who has believed our report?' explains the mixed response to the gospel (Rom 10:16).
13713: God will make Israel jealous by those who are not a nation: a theme Paul develops in chapter 11.
13714: Romans 10:9 is a simple formula: say a prayer acknowledging Jesus and you are saved, whatever follows.
13715: The confession 'Jesus is Lord' is a public, life-shaping allegiance to the risen king, believed in the heart. Scholars like Matthew Bates stress allegiance; Reformed scholars stress trust, not performance. Both reject a formula disconnected from a changed life.
13716: The Olive Tree: God Has Not Rejected His People
13717: Has God rejected his people? By no means: Paul himself is an Israelite, and there is a remnant chosen by grace, as in Elijah's day. Israel's stumbling is not final; through it salvation has come to the Gentiles, to make Israel jealous. Gentiles are wild olive branches grafted into Israel's tree and must not boast over the natural branches. A partial hardening has come on Israel until the fullness of the Gentiles comes in, and so all Israel will be saved, for the gifts and calling of God are irrevocable. Paul ends in a hymn of praise to God's unsearchable wisdom.
13718: Paul addresses Gentile believers directly here (11:13). After the expulsion under Claudius, Gentile believers may have come to lead the house churches and to regard returning Jewish believers as relics. Paul pushes hard against this. Tragically, later church history often did exactly what Paul warned against, which is why this chapter is central to modern Jewish-Christian dialogue.
13719: Grafting was ordinary farming knowledge around the Mediterranean, though normally cultivated branches were grafted onto wild stock. Paul deliberately reverses it ('contrary to nature', 11:24), stressing that Gentile inclusion is pure gift. Boasting (11:18) again reflects an honour culture in which groups competed for status. The closing doxology mirrors Jewish prayers of praise.
13720: The olive tree was an image for Israel (Jer 11:16; Hos 14:6). Elijah's complaint and God's answer about the 7,000 (1 Kgs 19:10-18) shows that God always keeps a faithful remnant. 'The deliverer will come from Zion' (Isa 59:20-21) and the promise to take away sins (Isa 27:9; Jer 31:33-34) express Israel's hope of restoration. Paul's confidence that God will not abandon Israel echoes Jeremiah: only if heaven can be measured will God reject Israel (Jer 31:37). The doxology quotes Isaiah 40 and Job.
13721: Gentile believers were sharply warned: you stand only by faith, do not be arrogant, you could be cut off too. Jewish believers would be greatly encouraged: their people were not finished, and Paul expected a future in which 'all Israel' would be saved. Both groups were invited to see their story as one tree.
13722: Romans 11 is one of the strongest biblical correctives to Christian anti-Judaism. Whatever one thinks about how 'all Israel' will be saved, Gentile Christians are commanded not to boast over Jews and to recognise their dependence on Israel's root. Many churches have revised their teaching about Judaism since the Holocaust partly because of this chapter.
13723: God reserves 7,000 who did not bow to Baal: the remnant 'chosen by grace' (Rom 11:4-5).
13724: A redeemer will come to Zion and God's covenant and Spirit will remain, quoted in Rom 11:26-27.
13725: Israel as a green olive tree, the image behind Paul's olive tree.
13726: Israel will not cease as a nation before God while the sun and moon endure: God's covenant faithfulness.
13727: 'Who has known the mind of the LORD?' quoted in the closing doxology (Rom 11:34).
13728: The church has replaced Israel; God's promises to the Jewish people now belong to Christians.
13729: Paul writes Romans 11 to stop Gentile believers from thinking that. God has not rejected his people; Gentiles are grafted into Israel's tree; God's calling is irrevocable. Scholars debate who 'all Israel' is (ethnic Israel in the future, as Moo and Schreiner hold, or the whole people of God, as Wright holds), but not that Gentile arrogance is forbidden.
13731: In view of God's mercies (the whole argument of chapters 1-11), Paul urges believers to present their bodies as a living sacrifice, their reasonable worship, and to be transformed by the renewing of their minds rather than conformed to this age. No one should think too highly of themselves; they are one body with different gifts given by grace. Love must be genuine: honour one another, welcome strangers, bless persecutors, live in harmony, never take revenge, and overcome evil with good.
13732: With the theological argument complete, Paul turns to the life of the community. The Roman house churches were small, socially mixed groups, meeting in homes and apartment blocks (insulae). Some members were wealthy enough to host; many were slaves, freedpeople or artisans. Paul's appeal is to the whole community together: 'your bodies' (plural) is one 'sacrifice' (singular).
13733: Rome was full of temples and animal sacrifices; worship meant offering something dead on an altar. Paul calls for living sacrifices: the whole of daily life. Honour was a limited good that people competed for; Paul says 'outdo one another in showing honour' (12:10), reversing the competition. Hospitality to strangers (philoxenia) was vital for travelling believers. The 'body' was a familiar political image: the Roman fable of Menenius Agrippa used it to keep plebeians in their place, while Paul uses it to give every member a gift and a role.
13734: Sacrifice language comes from Israel's temple and the Psalms, where God desires a broken heart and thanksgiving (Ps 51:16-17; Ps 50:14). Paul's ethics are drawn from Torah and wisdom: 'Vengeance is mine, I will repay' (Deut 32:35) and 'If your enemy is hungry, feed him' (Prov 25:21-22). This continues Jewish teaching on mercy to enemies, not a break from it. 'Not conformed to this age' reflects the Jewish two-ages framework: this present age and the age to come.
